title: Noel Tata Deserves Answers From the Tata Sons Board

 Noel Tata has asked for a response within seven days of his letter. He has also made clear that he does not accept the validity of the September 17 resolution and has reserved his rights and remedies. Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata during the 'Invest Maharashtra' event, in Mumbai, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Photo: PTI. Advertisement Tata group patriarch Noel Tata’s latest letter to the directors of Tata Sons Private Limited is more than a challenge to the validity of a board resolution. It is a demand for answers from an institution whose reputation has been built on trust, integrity and corporate governance for over a century which is now lying in the dust – thanks to the Tata rebels.
 The questions he has raised from Tata Sons board deserve a clear response. Not merely because Noel Tata chairs Tata Trusts, but also because he is entrusted with preserving a legacy built over generations by his forefathers.
 Tata is being criminally destroyed, and no business leader dares say a word.
 How long will you stay silent? Until they own you?
 Indian business is not Modi and Shah's plaything. You lack courage. We don't. We will ensure justice for these crimes.
 — Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) October 28, 2026 
In his letter dated October 26, 2026, Noel Tata challenged the validity of the September 17 Tata Sons board resolution concerning N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as executive chairman. He questions whether the company’s Articles of Association were followed, seeks the preservation of records and raises concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
 These are serious issues. The board must address them on their merits rather than allow the dispute to become a contest of personalities. The Board must answer why Chandrasekaran took a U-turn after deciding to quit on August 12 and why the board decided to go against the wishes of Tata Trusts.
 Noel Tata’s letter identifies decisions that, he says, require an affirmative vote from Tata Trusts under Article 121 of the company’s Articles of Association. These include the continuation or re-designation of the executive chairman outside the prescribed provisions.
 Advertisement 
 He writes:
 “Any appointment of an additional Director; any continuation or re-designation of the Executive Chairman otherwise than in accordance with Articles 118 and 121; any resolution that the Executive Chairman is not liable to retire by rotation; any increase in capital or issue or allotment of shares; any proposal to alter the Articles or to convert the Company; and any commitment to the Reserve Bank of India as to listing or a timetable for listing, each requires the affirmative vote under Article 121.”
 Advertisement 
 He also requests that such matters be considered only through a clearly specified agenda item, with papers circulated at least seven days before the meeting. He refers specifically to the September 17 meeting.
 The central question is whether the applicable provisions were followed when Chandrasekaran’s reappointment was considered. The independent directors must explain how they satisfied themselves that the decision complied with the company’s governing documents. What provisions did they rely on? How did they interpret the voting requirements? Were the prescribed procedures followed?
 Advertisement 
 Independent directors are expected to exercise independent judgement for the sake of all stakeholders. Their responsibility is not simply to support a board decision but to ensure that the process complies with applicable rules and serves the company’s interests.
 Advertisement 
 Their role has therefore come into question. If the procedure was followed, the board should be able to demonstrate that through the relevant records and a reasoned explanation. If it was not, the implications cannot be brushed aside by asserting that a resolution was passed. A judicial scrutiny of the recent decisions of Tata Sons board is necessary so that the stakeholders know the truth.
 The conflict-of-interest question 
 Perhaps the most consequential issue raised in Noel Tata’s letter concerns Venu Srinivasan’s position and the potential conflict arising from the reported commercial dealings between TVS Motor Company owned by Srinivasan and Hanno One, a company associated with Chandrasekaran’s family. The Trusts own 66 per cent stake in Tata Sons and have veto powers over the Tata Sons board decisions. Noel Tata and Srinivasan were representing the Trusts at Tata Sons board. Even though Srinivasan was barred from voting at the September 17th Tata Sons board meeting by Tata Trusts, he went ahead and voted for Chandra's re-appointment.
 The letter states that Srinivasan is chairman emeritus of TVS Motor and a member of Tata Sons’ Nomination and Remuneration Committee, which reviews the performance and remuneration of the executive chairman. Noel Tata says Srinivasan participated in the committee’s deliberations on September 3, 2026, and cast the vote of a director nominated under Article 104B on which the company relies for the resolution concerning Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.
 Noel Tata argues that a director nominated by a charitable trust owes fiduciary duties not only to the trust but also to its beneficiaries. He describes the required standard as “pure, unadulterated public interest”.
 The letter contends that this responsibility required Srinivasan to disclose to Tata Trusts and the board any relationship between his company and the family of the person whose reappointment he was called upon to assess. It also raises the question of whether he disclosed his participation in the unanimous resolution of Sir Dorabji Tata Trust dated August 13th, 2026, concerning Chandrasekaran’s tenure.
 These questions require a clear explanation of what was disclosed, to whom and when.
 The letter also refers to the company spokesperson’s public position that Hanno One’s incorporation had been disclosed in April 2025 to the companies of which Chandrasekaran is chairman, and that the transaction between TVS Motor and Hanno One was not required to be disclosed to Tata Sons.
 Noel Tata challenges whether the relevant dealings were disclosed to the board. He writes:
 “I do not recall any disclosure of these dealings being placed before the Board.”
 He then refers to the September 17 meeting, when the board noted disclosures of interest under Section 184(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. According to his letter, the disclosure recorded from Srinivasan concerned his having ceased to be a director of TVS group companies on June 10, 2026.
 No disclosure from Chandrasekaran or Srinivasan concerning Hanno One or its dealings with TVS Motor was noted, Noel Tata says, either under that agenda item or when the reappointment was considered.
 The board must address this directly. What information was available to the directors? Were the relevant relationships and dealings disclosed elsewhere? How were potential conflicts assessed before the reappointment was considered? Were the independent directors of Tata Sons aware of the conflict of interest?
 Noel Tata makes an important distinction between the technical application of company law and the broader responsibilities of directors. He writes:
 “Whether or not Sections 184(2) or 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 apply to a transaction between two third parties, every Director is bound to exercise independent judgment and to avoid a situation in which he has, or may have, a direct or indirect interest which conflicts, or may conflict, with the interests of the Company.”
 The issue, therefore, is not simply whether a transaction falls within a particular statutory disclosure requirement. It is also whether directors exercised independent judgement and adequately addressed potential conflicts.
 A commercial relationship does not, by itself, establish wrongdoing. Nor does the absence of a disclosure in the minutes cited conclusively establish that no disclosure was made elsewhere. Those questions must be examined against the relevant records.
 But the board should explain how it assessed the potential conflict and ensured that the directors concerned could discharge their responsibilities independently.
Records and judicial scrutiny 
 Noel Tata has requested the preservation of all records relating to the dispute, including notices, agendas and papers for the September 3 and September 17 meetings, the Board's web app’s logs and audit trail, communications between directors and the company, legal opinions and disclosures of interest.
 These documents could establish what was placed before the board, what directors knew and how the decision was reached. He has also called for every board and committee meeting to be recorded in full, with recordings preserved and made available to directors on request.
 The importance of an accurate record is clear. Confidentiality in board deliberations is legitimate, but it cannot substitute for accountability when the validity of a consequential decision is challenged.
 Noel Tata has asked for a response within seven days of his letter. He has also made clear that he does not accept the validity of the September 17 resolution and has reserved his rights and remedies.
 If the board cannot resolve the questions through a substantive response, judicial scrutiny may become necessary. A court could examine the Articles, meeting records, disclosures and applicable duties to determine whether the resolution was valid and whether any director failed to discharge a legal obligation.
 Such scrutiny would not automatically establish wrongdoing. But it could provide an authoritative determination if the dispute cannot be resolved internally.
 Also read: What Fuelled the Rebellion Within the Tatas 
 The independent directors should explain their reasoning rather than rely on the collective authority of the board. If they followed the rules, the records should help establish that. If questions remain, those questions deserve answers.
The Tata legacy is at stake 
 Tata Sons is not an ordinary holding company. Its reputation rests not only on its businesses but also on the institutional values associated with the Tata name.
 Noel Tata’s position as chairman of Tata Trusts gives the dispute wider significance, but the issue extends beyond his institutional role. It concerns whether Tata Sons’ governance standards remain robust when its leadership and the interpretation of its own rules are challenged.
 This should not be reduced to a contest between Noel Tata and Chandrasekaran or Venu Srinivasan. The central question is whether the company can demonstrate that its decisions comply with its governing documents and that its directors discharge their responsibilities with independence and integrity.
 The board must answer Noel Tata’s questions point by point. The independent directors must explain their reasoning. The potential conflict-of-interest concerns must be addressed through the relevant records and disclosures.
 Noel Tata deserves answers – not merely as chairman of Tata Trusts, but as someone entrusted with preserving a legacy built over generations. So do the stakeholders whose confidence depends on the integrity of Tata Sons.
 Preserving that legacy means demonstrating that the rules apply when the stakes are highest, that potential conflicts are taken seriously and that those entrusted with governance can account for their decisions.
 If the board can do that, it will strengthen the institution. If it cannot, the questions raised in Noel Tata’s letter may ultimately have to be answered in an open court.
 Dev Chatterjee is a senior journalist and co-author of  The Meltdown and India Inc’s Greatest Turnarounds .
